name: Linear Pottery culture
info: The Linear Pottery culture (LBK) was a Neolithic archaeological horizon of central Europe, c. 5500–4500 BC, whose farmers spread agriculture along the Danube, Elbe and Rhine and built the largest free-standing buildings of their time, the longhouses.

facts.homeland: Central Europe, chiefly the middle Danube, the upper and middle Elbe and the upper and middle Rhine, at its widest from the Paris Basin to the Dnieper; key sites include Vráble and Nitra in Slovakia, Bylany in the Czech Republic, Langweiler and Zwenkau (Eythra) in Germany, Brunn am Gebirge in Austria, Elsloo in the Netherlands and Flomborn, Hienheim and Rössen
facts.period: Early or Western LBK from conventionally 5500 BC (possibly 5700 BC); Music Note pottery from about 5200 BC; Stroke-ornamented ware 5000–4500 BC; the Eastern or Alföld LBK c. 5330–4940 BC; a late survival in Belgium as late as 4100 BC
facts.known: incised “linear band” pottery; timber longhouses up to 45 m long; the rapid spread of farming at about 4 km a year; emmer and einkorn wheat, peas and lentils; cattle and dairying; timber-lined wells; the mass graves of Talheim, Herxheim and Schöneck-Kilianstädten
facts.sources: Excavated settlements, cemeteries and wells; radiocarbon dates; the term Bandkeramik from Friedrich Klopfleisch and V. Gordon Childe’s Danubian; ancient DNA studies from 2005 onward; residue analysis of over 4,300 pots; the interpretations of Marija Gimbutas

t: The Linear Pottery culture spread about 1,500 km along the rivers in 360 years, about 4 km a year, and represents a major event in the spread of agriculture in Europe.
Its longhouses, 5.5 to 7.0 m wide and sometimes 45 m long, were the largest free-standing buildings in the world at the time.
Mass graves such as the Talheim Death Pit and Herxheim overturned an earlier view of the culture as peaceful and unfortified.
dyk: A 2022 study of residues from over 4,300 vessels at 70 LBK sites found traces of milk at about 65% of them, some dating as early as 7,400 years ago.
ev: The early Linear Pottery culture developed on the middle Danube, possibly as early as 5700 BC
The classical Alföld Linear Pottery culture appeared north of the Körös culture
The LBK reached the Netherlands while Music Note pottery appeared in Austria
The settlement at Vráble reached its peak with perhaps 70 longhouses and up to 1,725 people
The killings of the Talheim Death Pit took place, among the earliest evidence of organised violence in Neolithic Europe
Stroke-ornamented ware developed in central Europe and spread down the Vistula and Elbe
A timber trackway was laid across the Campemoor bog in Lower Saxony

sections.origins:
The Linear Pottery culture, from the German Linearbandkeramik (LBK), is a major archaeological horizon of the European Neolithic, flourishing c. 5500–4500 BC. It began in the regions of densest settlement on the middle Danube, in Bohemia, Moravia and Hungary, and spread some 1,500 km along the rivers in 360 years. At its greatest it reached from the Paris Basin to the Dnieper, but it stayed inland: the northern coasts were left to Mesolithic peoples living on the Atlantic salmon runs.

Its origins are debated. The oldest theory derives it from the Starčevo-Körös culture of Serbia and Hungary; at Brunn am Gebirge near Vienna, Starčevo-type pottery gives way to LBK pottery in the same longhouse settlement. A second theory sees it developing from local Mesolithic cultures, citing a gap of up to 500 years after farming reached southern Hungary. A third points to influence from the steppe. Ancient DNA from 2005 onward links its people to Neolithic Anatolian farmers, with Y-DNA mostly of haplogroup G2a, and suggests their descendants have been part of the European population for more than 7,000 years.
sections.society:
The LBK people settled on river terraces with fertile loess and grew a mix of crops in small plots, a “garden type of civilization” in Gimbutas’s phrase. Their main crops were emmer, einkorn, peas and lentils, with hemp and flax for rope and cloth. They raised cattle above all, with some goats and pigs, and hunted deer and wild boar. A study of Vráble found that fields were used as pastures to make manure, and a GIS study of the Wetterau concluded that grazing land, not arable land, limited settlement there.

The household lived in the longhouse, a rectangular timber building 5.5 to 7.0 m wide and of varying length; one at Bylany was 45 m long. Villages of five to eight houses lay about 20 m apart, and nearby villages formed settlement cells. Vráble in Slovakia had perhaps 70 longhouses standing at once and up to 1,725 people around 5100 BC. Pottery found mainly in women’s graves suggests women made it, and Gimbutas inferred a matrilocal pattern. Flint from southern Poland and obsidian from the Bükk and Tatra mountains were traded across the whole range.
sections.beliefs:
As with all prehistoric cultures, the beliefs of the Linear Pottery people are poorly understood, and how far they formed a system is debated. Marija Gimbutas read the culture within a mother goddess model inherited from the Palaeolithic, arguing that the female principle predominated and that burial pits lined with stone, clay or plaster may have stood for eggs, the dead returning there to await rebirth. Some of the figurines, however, are androgynous rather than female.

Burial practice varied. Women and children were buried under the floors of houses, while the remains of adult men are missing from them. Cemeteries came into use at about 5000 BC, holding 20 to 200 graves in groups that seem to follow kinship; both cremation and burial of the body in a flexed position were practised. Only about 30% of graves have goods: men’s held stone celts, flint tools and Spondylus shells from the Aegean, women’s most of the pottery and containers of ochre. Whether these were gifts or possessions, they point to differences in standing. At the end of the culture, Herxheim and Vráble show marked changes in ritual practice.
sections.arts:
The culture is named after its pottery: simple cups, bowls, vases and jugs, at first without handles and later with pierced lugs, bases and necks. Its decoration imitates and refines the painted spirals and bands of Starčevo-Körös ware with incised lines, hence “linear” band ware, though the lines are mostly not straight. The middle phase brought Music Note pottery, whose lines are broken by punctures like musical notes, and the late phase Stroke-ornamented ware, in which rows of punctures replace the lines. Analysis shows that each house had its own pottery tradition.

The people were also skilled builders in timber. Longhouse walls were of wattle and daub, sometimes with split logs, under slanted thatched roofs carried on rows of posts, oak being preferred. Timber-lined wells built layer by layer show sophisticated carpentry, and timber trackways crossed bogs, as at Campemoor in Lower Saxony around 4630–4550 BC. The tool kit used flint and obsidian, with no metal: sickles set with flint blades, the ground-stone “shoe-last celt” used as an adze, and flint-tipped augers.
sections.exchange:
The Linear Pottery culture spread through lands partly held by hunter-gatherers. In the Netherlands it arrived about 5200 BC among people already producing some food, and the La Hoguette culture to the north-west developed farming of its own; Neolithic and Mesolithic peoples evidently did not exclude each other. The trade in flint and obsidian from specialised mining settlements to every LBK region is a strong argument for a unity across the culture’s scattered pockets.

Conflict was part of its history. The Talheim Death Pit in southern Germany, c. 5000 BC, is among the earliest known evidence of organised violence in Neolithic Europe; study of its skeletons suggests men of neighbouring groups fought to capture women. The massacre of Schletz happened at about the same time, at a fortified site. At Schöneck-Kilianstädten 26 adults and children were killed by blows to the head or arrows, and Herxheim held the scattered remains of at least 450 people. Other suggested causes are vengeance, conflict over land and resources, and slave raiding. Some fortifications facing lands of the older inhabitants were used only briefly.
sections.legacy:
The population rose fast during the culture, a phenomenon called the Neolithic demographic transition. Bocquet-Appel attributed it to shorter intervals between births, and its end to higher mortality, perhaps from new diseases spread by closer contact. After 5000 BC came a population decline of “enormous magnitude”, with levels staying low for the next 1,500 years. In the Wetterau the population fell back to its first level while arable land was still free.

A number of cultures replaced the LBK across its range, without a one-to-one match between its variants and its successors: among them the Hinkelstein, Großgartach, Rössen, Lengyel, Cucuteni–Trypillia and Boian cultures. In eastern Hungary the late groups passed into the Tisza-Hérpály-Csöszhalom complex and the Tiszapolgár culture. Genetic studies indicate that the descendants of LBK people have lived in Europe for more than 7,000 years and are part of the present-day population. New finds continue: in 2019 two large rondel complexes were discovered east of the Vistula near Toruń in Poland.

summary: The Linear Pottery culture carried farming across central Europe from about 5500 BC, its people of Anatolian farming descent growing emmer and einkorn, keeping cattle for meat and milk and living in timber longhouses. Named for its incised pottery, it ended around 4500 BC after a period of violence and population decline, and was followed by many regional cultures.
